939.title: The Dalai Lamas
939.hook: the line of Dalai Lamas, and the Fifth, who unified Tibet
939.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, tulkus are searched for and recognized after a teacher's death, then raised and trained in a monastery; the Dalai Lamas belong to the Gelug school and are regarded as emanations of Avalokiteshvara, Chenrezig.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two canons: the Kangyur on one shelf, the Tengyur on the other. Your line was words and commentaries. Did you catch someone's take dressed up as the words themselves? Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

A small child in a farmhouse is shown a tray of objects: prayer beads, a walking stick, a small drum. Some belonged to a teacher who has died. Some did not. The visitors who brought the tray are monks. They are watching which ones the child reaches for. Stories like this are told about how a new teacher in a line is found. One of these lines carries a title known far beyond Tibet. Today, tulku.
screen: `A CHILD AND A TRAY OF OBJECTS.` → `MONKS WATCHING.` → `HOW A LINE CONTINUES.`

segments.voice: First, what a line like this is. In Tibetan Buddhism, a great teacher who dies may be recognized again in a child, who is found, tested, trained, and then takes up the same work. Such a teacher is called a tulku. The tradition holds that this happens out of compassion: a teacher chooses to come back to keep helping. The Dalai Lamas are one of these lines, belonging to the Gelug school. Second, what Tibetans see in them. Tibetan Buddhists regard the Dalai Lamas as an emanation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, whom Tibetans call Chenrezig. So, Tibetans say, to honor a Dalai Lama is to honor compassion itself, wearing a human face. Third, the Fifth. He's often called the Great Fifth. In his time, Tibet had been divided among rival rulers and rival schools. With the help of a Mongol ruler who backed him, the Fifth Dalai Lama came to lead a unified Tibetan government, as both its spiritual and its political head. He was also a scholar and a writer, and he began the building we'll visit tomorrow. Fourth, honesty about the story. Tibetan Buddhists hold the line as compassion at work, and it has also lived inside real history: alliances, wars, rival claims, hard choices. Tibetan histories tell it with many of those turns. Holding both, the compassion and the politics, is part of telling it fairly. The line continues today. Each Dalai Lama is counted by number, so each number carries the whole line behind it.
screen: `A TEACHER RECOGNIZED AGAIN: A TULKU.` · `CHENREZIG, WEARING A HUMAN FACE.` · `THE GREAT FIFTH UNITES TIBET.` · `COMPASSION, INSIDE REAL HISTORY.` · then, large: `A LINE OF TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one name in a lineage. A lineage can be a line of teachers, or a family, or a craft passed hand to hand. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who taught you something, and then, if you know it, the person who taught them. Say the two names silently, one after the other, like beads on a string. If no name comes, use Chenrezig, the name Tibetans give to compassion in bodhisattva form. Then rest, and let the breath be the thread. The bell holds the time.
Tulku. A great teacher reborn in a child to continue the work, the kind of line the Dalai Lamas, in the Gelug school, belong to. Today's word.
Your line: a line of teachers. Today, thank one person in your own line: a teacher, a mentor, an older relative, out loud or in a short message. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

940.title: The Potala
940.hook: the great palace on the hill in Lhasa
940.howItsDone: Pilgrims in Lhasa walk the circuit around the Potala's hill clockwise, often spinning prayer wheels and reciting mantras, and visit its chapels and the tombs of past Dalai Lamas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tulku, the Dalai Lamas, and the Great Fifth who came to lead a unified Tibet. Your line was a line of teachers. Who in your own line did you thank? Day nine hundred forty.

Walls, white and then deep red, rising out of the rock as if the hill grew them. Windows in long rows, stair after stair zigzagging up the face, gold roofs at the very top catching the thin, bright air. Below it, the city of Lhasa. Pilgrims walk around the hill's foot, turning prayer wheels, and look up. For a long time this was the home of the Dalai Lamas, and the place from which Tibet was governed. Today, the Potala.
screen: `WHITE WALLS, THEN RED.` → `GOLD ROOFS IN THIN AIR.` → `PILGRIMS CIRCLE BELOW.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition says Potala comes from Potalaka, the mountain where, in Buddhist texts, Avalokiteshvara dwells. Yesterday we heard that Tibetans regard the Dalai Lamas as an emanation of Chenrezig, Avalokiteshvara. So the palace was named for his mountain. The home on the hill is the bodhisattva's mountain, brought to Lhasa. Second, the builder. The Great Fifth began the palace as his seat. Tradition says a palace of Tibet's early king Songtsen Gampo once stood on the same hill, so the new building stood on old ground. Third, the two colors. The White Palace held the offices and living rooms: where the work of government and daily life went on. The Red Palace, rising in the middle, is given over to religion: chapels, halls, and the golden tombs of past Dalai Lamas, built as stupas. So the building holds the two roles we met yesterday, side by side. The worldly work in white. The spiritual heart in red. Fourth, what a palace on a hill does. It stands where the city can see it. Someone carrying water, someone haggling at a market stall, someone walking home at dusk, can turn and see it. A building like that becomes a reminder, whether you ask for one or not. Some pilgrims walk the circuit around the hill, keeping it on their right, the way Buddhists walk around a stupa. They don't have to go in. Circling it is the practice.
screen: `POTALAKA: AVALOKITESHVARA'S MOUNTAIN.` · `THE GREAT FIFTH BUILDS ON OLD GROUND.` · `WHITE FOR WORK, RED FOR PRAYER.` · `WHERE THE CITY CAN SEE IT.` · then, large: `THE PALACE ON THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the palace on the hill. Settle, and breathe. Imagine you're standing in a street of Lhasa, busy with your own errand. Then you lift your eyes, and there it is above the roofs: white walls, then red, the gold at the top. Stay with that view for a few breaths. Then look back down to the street, and the errand. Whenever your mind wanders, lift your eyes again, and let the hill be there. The bell holds the time.
The Potala. The palace on the hill in Lhasa, named for Avalokiteshvara's mountain, white for the work of governing and red for prayer. Today's word.
Your line: the palace on the hill. Today, choose one thing you can see from where you work or live, a tree, a roof, a window, and let it be your reminder to breathe. Day nine hundred forty.

941.title: Mongolia
941.hook: the Mongol ruler Altan Khan gives the title Dalai Lama
941.howItsDone: Buddhism in Mongolia follows the Tibetan tradition, especially the Gelug school; monastic chanting there is commonly in Tibetan, and the Dalai Lamas are revered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Potala: white for the work of governing, red for prayer. Your line was the palace on the hill. What did you choose to look up at? Day nine hundred forty-one.

Two days ago we heard the title Dalai Lama, and the Fifth who carried it. But where does the title itself come from? Not from Tibet. It comes from the grasslands to the north, from felt tents and herds of horses and a ruler with an army. A Tibetan monk named Sonam Gyatso traveled to meet a Mongol prince called Altan Khan. The prince listened, was moved, and gave the monk a new name. Today, Mongolia.
screen: `A TITLE FROM THE NORTH.` → `A MONK MEETS A KHAN.` → `A NEW NAME IS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the meeting. Altan Khan was a powerful Mongol ruler. He invited Sonam Gyatso, a leading teacher of the Gelug school, to come north, and the two met. Tibetan and Mongol accounts both remember it as a turning point: the Khan took up the teaching, and it put down deep roots among the Mongols. Second, the title. The Khan honored the monk with the name Dalai. In Mongolian, dalai means ocean. And notice: the monk's own Tibetan name, Gyatso, also means ocean. The Khan simply said it in his own language. The title is often rendered ocean of wisdom: a teacher whose understanding is as wide and deep as the sea. Third, a line looking backward. Sonam Gyatso was already the heir of earlier teachers in his line, so the title was given back to them too. That is why the first to receive the title in person is counted not as the first Dalai Lama but as the third. Names in a lineage can reach backward as well as forward. Fourth, what it opened. From then on Mongolia and Tibet were tied together by teachers, students, pilgrims and politics. Mongol monks went south to study in Tibetan monasteries. Mongol rulers backed Tibetan teachers, as we heard with the Great Fifth. And monasteries rose across the steppe. A title that began as one ruler's honor became the name of a whole line. Not a word from Tibet, but a word from the grasslands, given in thanks.
screen: `ALTAN KHAN INVITES A TEACHER.` · `DALAI: OCEAN, IN MONGOLIAN.` · `THE TITLE REACHES BACKWARD.` · `MONGOLIA AND TIBET, TIED TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE OCEAN OF WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Mongolia on a map, in your mind or on a screen after the bell. Today's Mongolia sits between Russia to the north and China to the south, with no coast at all, and Altan Khan's own lands lay just south of it, in what is now China. A people far from any sea, and their word for ocean became the name of a line of teachers. Settle, and breathe. With each breath, picture the grasslands rolling out wide in every direction, like water. Let the mind be that wide for a little while. The bell holds the time.
Mongolia. The land of the Mongols, whose ruler Altan Khan gave Sonam Gyatso the title Dalai, ocean, and where the teaching put down deep roots. Today's word.
Your line: the ocean of wisdom. Today, find out what one name means, your own, a friend's, or your street's, the way gyatso and dalai turned out to mean the same thing. Day nine hundred forty-one.

942.title: Bamiyan
942.hook: the great Buddhas carved in an Afghan cliff, and destroyed
942.howItsDone: Buddhists and others remember the Bamiyan Buddhas as a lost holy site and part of the world's shared heritage; the empty niches and the painted caves around them are now protected and visited.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mongolia, where a Khan gave a teacher the title Dalai, ocean. Your line was the ocean of wisdom. Whose name did you look up? Day nine hundred forty-two.

In a green valley in the mountains of Afghanistan, a visitor stands at the foot of a tall cliff of soft, tan rock and looks up. Cut into its face are two enormous hollows, arched at the top, each the shape of a standing figure. Inside them, nothing. Rubble at the bottom, sky on the stone. For a long time those hollows held two great Buddhas, standing, carved from the cliff itself, looking out over the valley. Now they hold their own absence. Today, Bamiyan.
screen: `A CLIFF IN AN AFGHAN VALLEY.` → `TWO HOLLOWS, SHAPED LIKE FIGURES.` → `INSIDE, NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, what stood there. The Bamiyan valley sat on the old roads between India and Central Asia, the roads monks and merchants walked. Buddhist communities carved the two standing Buddhas into the cliff, along with caves around them where monks lived and meditated, some painted on the inside. Second, a witness. We've met the pilgrim Xuanzang, who walked from China to India for texts. On his way, he passed through Bamiyan, and in his record of the journey he describes a great standing Buddha carved from the rock, its gold shining, and monasteries with monks. His few lines let us see the valley through the eyes of someone who stood there when it was alive. Third, the loss. The region's people changed faiths over the centuries, and the statues stayed, worn by weather, time and earlier damage, their faces long gone, but standing. Then, within living memory, the Taliban, who ruled Afghanistan at the time, declared the statues idols and destroyed them with explosives. People of many faiths around the world, Muslims among them, had asked that they be spared. They were not. Fourth, what remains. The two empty niches are still there, the shape of the Buddhas pressed into the rock like a footprint. And the Buddha himself taught impermanence: that everything put together comes apart. That teaching doesn't make the loss small. It's still a loss, and people still grieve it. But the niches say something too. You can see exactly what was there, by the shape of where it's gone.
screen: `TWO BUDDHAS ON THE OLD ROADS.` · `XUANZANG SAW THEM SHINING.` · `DESTROYED, DESPITE PLEAS TO SPARE THEM.` · `THE SHAPE OF WHERE IT'S GONE.` · then, large: `THE EMPTY NICHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one lost thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that's gone: a building you loved, a place that changed, an old photo, a voice. Don't rush to fix the feeling. Just look at the shape it left, the way the niches hold the shape of the Buddhas. Say silently: I remember you. Then rest in the breath, and let the remembering be enough. The bell holds the time.
Bamiyan. The Afghan valley where two great Buddhas stood in the cliff, seen by Xuanzang, destroyed in our own time, and remembered in their empty niches. Today's word.
Your line: the empty niches. Today, when you notice something missing, a gap on a shelf, a chair, a name, pause for one breath and remember what was there. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: Dunhuang
943.hook: a sealed cave library in China, holding a printed Diamond Sutra that carries its own date
943.howItsDone: Copying, printing and giving away sutras has long been a way Buddhists make merit, often dedicated to parents or loved ones, as Wang Jie did; the Diamond Sutra is still chanted and studied, especially in East Asian Buddhism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bamiyan, where two Buddhas stood in a cliff and two hollows remember them. Your line was the empty niches. What gap did you stop and remember? Day nine hundred forty-three.

A caretaker is clearing sand from a cave temple at the edge of the desert in western China. Along one painted passage, he notices a crack in the wall. Behind it, the plaster is hollow. He breaks through, and finds a small room packed from floor to ceiling with scrolls, bundles, banners and paintings, sealed in and forgotten for a long time, dry as the desert kept them. Among them, rolled up, is a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra. Today, Dunhuang.
screen: `A CAVE TEMPLE IN THE DESERT.` → `A CRACK, A HOLLOW WALL.` → `A ROOM FULL OF SCROLLS.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Dunhuang was an oasis town where the roads from China met the roads west, part of the same web of old roads that ran past Bamiyan. Near it, Buddhists cut cave after cave into a cliff, the Mogao caves, and painted them from floor to ceiling with Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and stories from the sutras. Second, the hidden room. Nobody knows for certain why it was sealed. Some suggest it was a storeroom for worn-out texts too holy to throw away; others suggest it was hidden from danger. The sources are silent, and that's worth saying plainly. What is certain is what it held: writings in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit and other languages, Buddhist and not. Third, the scroll. It's a printed Diamond Sutra, made by carving whole pages into wooden blocks, inking them, and pressing paper onto them. It opens with a picture of the Buddha teaching. And at its end, a short line tells us who made it and why: a man named Wang Jie had it made, on behalf of his two parents, to be given away freely. Then it gives the day, the month and the year, by the Chinese calendar of the time. That small line is why the British Library, which keeps it now, calls it the earliest dated printed book. Fourth, what that means. Other printing may be older. But this one tells us when. A son, honoring his parents, wanted the teaching to travel. It's still traveling. How the scroll left Dunhuang is part of the story too: explorers carried large parts of the library away, to Europe and beyond, and people still argue over whether that was rescue or taking.
screen: `AN OASIS ON THE OLD ROADS.` · `A ROOM SEALED, NO ONE KNOWS WHY.` · `WANG JIE, FOR HIS TWO PARENTS.` · `IT TELLS US WHEN.` · then, large: `THE OLDEST PRINTED BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an old book. If there's one near you, a family Bible, a grandmother's cookbook, a school prize, open it after the bell and look for a name or a date written inside. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture a page someone made long ago, so that someone else could read it. Let the breath slow. Think of the hands that carved it, inked it, carried it, kept it. You're one of the readers they were hoping for. The bell holds the time.
Dunhuang. The oasis where a sealed cave held a printed Diamond Sutra, made by Wang Jie for his parents, with its own date at the end. Today's word.
Your line: the oldest printed book. Today, write a name and today's date inside something you'll keep, a book, a card, a photo, for whoever finds it next. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: Vietnamese Zen
944.hook: the Truc Lam school founded by a king who became a monk
944.howItsDone: Vietnamese Buddhists honor Tran Nhan Tong as the founder of the Truc Lam school of Thien; pilgrims climb Mount Yen Tu to its pagodas, and Truc Lam monasteries teach seated meditation alongside everyday mindful work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dunhuang, and a printed Diamond Sutra that Wang Jie had made for his parents. Your line was the oldest printed book. Where did you write a name and a date? Day nine hundred forty-four.

A crown, set down on a table. Royal robes, folded. A king has held his country together through war, and has a son ready to rule. And instead of staying on the throne until the end, he hands it over. In time he puts on a monk's plain robe and climbs a mountain called Yen Tu, in the north of Vietnam. There, among the trees, he starts a school of Zen that would carry the name of a bamboo grove. Today, Vietnamese Zen.
screen: `A CROWN SET DOWN.` → `A PLAIN ROBE PUT ON.` → `UP THE MOUNTAIN OF YEN TU.`

segments.voice: First, Zen's name in Vietnam. The same meditation school we met in China as Chan, in Korea as Seon, and in Japan as Zen, is called Thien in Vietnam. All of these names go back to the Sanskrit word for meditation, dhyana. Thien had already been in Vietnam a long while, in several lines of teachers, before our king. Second, the king. His name was Tran Nhan Tong. Vietnamese histories remember him as a ruler who led his kingdom through hard years of war, and then gave the throne to his son while he was still able to rule. Some years later he became a monk on Mount Yen Tu, and there he founded the Truc Lam school. Truc Lam means bamboo grove. Third, what the school taught. Truc Lam gathered Vietnam's lines of Thien into one, a school that was Vietnam's own. And its teaching was direct. Verses attributed to the king say that the Buddha is not somewhere far away, but in your own heart, and that you can practice the Way while living in the world: working, eating, resting. When the mind is quiet, everyday life becomes the practice. Fourth, the shape of the story. A man who held a throne chose a robe, a mountain, and a simpler day. The Truc Lam school honors him as its first patriarch, and the pagodas of Yen Tu still draw pilgrims up the mountain. The point isn't that everyone should leave everything. It's that he did leave something, and in the story, less was enough.
screen: `CHAN, SEON, ZEN, AND THIEN.` · `TRAN NHAN TONG GIVES UP THE THRONE.` · `TRUC LAM: THE BAMBOO GROVE.` · `THE BUDDHA IN YOUR OWN HEART.` · then, large: `THE KING BECAME A MONK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: simplify one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of your day as a room with too much in it. Look around slowly, and find one thing you could set down, the way the king set down his crown: a task that isn't yours, a worry you keep picking up, one app, one errand, one extra yes. Don't do anything about it yet. Just hold it, and imagine putting it on the table. Then rest with the breath, a little lighter. The bell holds the time.
Vietnamese Zen. Thien, and the Truc Lam school, the bamboo grove, founded on Mount Yen Tu by a king who became a monk. Today's word.
Your line: the king became a monk. Today, actually set down the one thing you found: cancel it, hand it over, or let it wait until tomorrow. Day nine hundred forty-four.

945.title: The first Western translators
945.hook: Burnouf, Müller, Rhys Davids bring the texts into French and English
945.howItsDone: Readers of Buddhism in the West still use the Pali Text Society's editions and translations, and the old public-domain translations by Max Müller and the Rhys Davids remain freely available and widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vietnamese Zen, and Tran Nhan Tong on Mount Yen Tu. Your line was the king became a monk. What did you set down? Day nine hundred forty-five.

"All that we are is the result of what we have thought." That sentence opens the Dhammapada, in the English of a scholar named Max Müller. Before translators like him, a reader in Paris or London who wanted to know what the Buddha taught often had to piece it together from travelers' tales and secondhand reports. Then a handful of scholars sat down with Sanskrit and Pali, and began. Today, Max Müller.
screen: `A LINE THAT OPENS A BOOK.` → `TRAVELERS' TALES AND GUESSES.` → `A HANDFUL OF SCHOLARS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: First, Eugène Burnouf, in Paris. Sanskrit manuscripts from Nepal reached him, and he read them closely: he translated the Lotus Sutra into French and wrote a long introduction to the history of Indian Buddhism. Scholars after him built on that book. Second, Max Müller, a German-born scholar who worked at Oxford. He translated the Dhammapada into English, and he edited a great series of translations called the Sacred Books of the East, which brought texts from many traditions to English readers. The Dhammapada opens, in his words: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Third, Thomas Rhys Davids. He worked for the British government in Sri Lanka, learned Pali there from Buddhist monks, and came home convinced the Pali texts deserved a careful edition. He founded the Pali Text Society to print and translate them, and his wife, Caroline Rhys Davids, became a translator and scholar in her own right. The sutta quotations in this path come from translations like theirs. Fourth, an honest frame. These translators worked inside empires, and they sometimes read Buddhism through their own assumptions. Their words are old now, and later translators have corrected them in places. But they also learned from Asian teachers and monks, and they opened a door. A line from a Sanskrit manuscript out of Nepal, or a palm leaf in Sri Lanka, could now be read in a kitchen in Ohio. And a look back at the week: a line of teachers, the palace on the hill, the ocean of wisdom, the empty niches, the oldest printed book, a king who became a monk, and now, into English.
